Neonatal Eastern grey kangaroos emerge after a relatively brief gestation period of approximately 36.4 days [tg = approximately 36.4 days], when measured at a maternal core body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], a remarkably short intrauterine phase even among marsupials. The newborn joey is minuscule at birth, weighing merely 0.8 grams [Wwb = 0.8 grams], and its head length at this stage measures only 0.88 centimeters [Lb = 0.88 centimeters]. This extreme altriciality is characteristic of the macropodid lineage, where the neonate must undertake an arduous climb from the birth canal to the pouch unaided by the mother. The joey then attaches to a teat, where it begins a protracted period of dependent development. Initial mass gain is slow, but the trajectory accelerates as the young animal matures within the protective environment of the pouch, relying entirely on maternal milk for its nutritional requirements during these early weeks of life.

The suckling juvenile undergoes a substantial developmental program before achieving nutritional independence. Weaning, defined as the cessation of lactation and the complete transition to a herbivorous diet, occurs at an average of 319 days [tx = 319 days] since birth, with this developmental milestone measured under a stable body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]. At this critical juncture, the young kangaroo has achieved a wet weight of approximately 6500 grams [Wwx = approximately 6500 grams] and a corresponding head length of 13.0 centimeters . The head length at weaning is a useful morphometric indicator of overall skeletal development, reflecting the substantial neural and cranial growth that has occurred during the extended period of maternal care. This relatively late weaning age is consistent with the slow life-history schedule typical of large-bodied macropodids inhabiting unpredictable environments.

The transition from juvenile to reproductive adult is marked by the attainment of sexual maturity, a gradual physiological process rather than a discrete event. For the Eastern grey kangaroo, puberty is reached at 639 days [tp = 639 days] since birth, as determined under a body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]. At the onset of this life-history stage, individuals exhibit a wet weight of approximately 17400 grams [Wwp = approximately 17400 grams] and a head length of about 16.4 centimeters [Lp = about 16.4 centimeters]. The head length at puberty, while substantial, still falls short of the ultimate adult size, indicating that somatic growth continues well after reproductive capacity is established. This decoupling of skeletal maturation from reproductive activation allows females to allocate resources to their own continued body growth even as they begin to produce offspring, a strategy common among long-lived herbivores where larger body size confers significant fitness advantages.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of an adult macropodid's resting metabolism, measured at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], an adult female Eastern grey kangaroo weighing approximately 26.4 kilograms exhibits an oxygen consumption rate of 94.6 milliliters per minute ; this value represents the basal metabolic expenditure required to sustain vital functions. The energetic demands of lactation are substantial, and field estimates indicate that the average yearly milk production for this species, expressed as the daily energetic yield of milk transferred to the offspring, amounts to approximately 72,800,000 joules per day  when assessed at the same maternal core temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. The ultimate adult wet weight, or the asymptotic body mass attained in the wild, reaches about 35000 grams [Wwi = about 35000 grams]. The head length of a fully grown individual ultimately stabilizes at 18.5 centimeters [Li = 18.5 centimeters], though exceptionally large males may approach 20.2 centimeters under optimal conditions, a length exceeding the typical asymptotic value.

The maximum reproductive rate observed under favorable environmental conditions corresponds to a single offspring produced annually [Ri = a single offspring produced annually], recorded at a body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]. This low fecundity is balanced by an impressively long lifespan; the maximum documented longevity for the species reaches 25 years [am = 25 years], as confirmed in wild populations and at the same temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]. This extended life expectancy, combined with delayed maturation and low annual reproductive output, classifies Macropus giganteus as a quintessential slow life-history strategist among Australian mammals. Populations are particularly vulnerable to environmental perturbations that affect adult survival, as the species cannot compensate for increased mortality through rapid recruitment. Comparative analyses with smaller macropodids, such as the red-necked wallaby, reveal that the Eastern grey kangaroo invests more heavily in somatic maintenance and survival at the expense of immediate reproductive output, a life-history trade-off that has proven successful across its broad geographical distribution.
